draft.title: Technology and global issues in setting up
card: A new business can use technology to build a customer database: a stored list of customer details, such as names, emails and past orders. It helps the business contact customers and see what they buy.
A database brings a choice about data. The business must collect only what it needs, keep it safe and follow Australian privacy law. A data breach can harm customers and the business's reputation.
A business can also deal with overseas suppliers or sell to overseas retailers. This can lower the cost of goods or reach more customers.
Global dealings bring risks. Exchange rates can change the price paid, shipping can be slow or costly, and it is harder to check a supplier's quality and standards.
draft.remember: Technology and global dealings can help a new business, but each brings choices about data, cost and risk.

a.q: Priya opens an online shop in Geelong and stores her customers' names, emails and orders. Which choice does this database mainly bring?
opts: How to keep the customer data safe and use it lawfully
How to avoid the effect of exchange rate changes
How to set the steps for handling a staff complaint
How to pick a supplier with the lowest delivery price
a.why: A customer database holds personal details, so the business must keep them safe and follow privacy law. Exchange rates matter when dealing overseas, not for a local database.
a.clue: Think about what is stored in the database.

b.q: Sam's Melbourne café switches to an overseas supplier of coffee machines because the price is 20% lower. Which risk should Sam weigh before agreeing?
opts: The cost in Australian dollars may rise if the rate moves
The supplier will be sure to deliver late
The lower price shows the machines are poor quality
Australian privacy law will apply to the machines
b.why: If the Australian dollar falls, the same overseas price costs more in Australian dollars, which can cancel the saving. A low price does not prove poor quality, and late delivery is possible but not certain.
b.clue: The supplier is paid in another country's money.

a.best: How to keep the customer data safe and use it lawfully

b.best: The cost in Australian dollars may rise if the rate moves

problems.detail: The card says a new business 'must collect only what it needs… and follow Australian privacy law' as if the Privacy Act's rules apply to every business. Most small businesses with annual turnover of $3 million or less are exempt from the Australian Privacy Principles, with some exceptions such as health providers and businesses that trade in personal information. A new business is usually in this group. The card should say 'should', or note that privacy law can apply.

The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('may'). Every distractor is an absolute claim ('will be sure to', 'will apply', 'shows'). A student could pick the answer by spotting the hedged option, without knowing about exchange rate risk.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card overstates privacy law, because most small businesses under $3 million turnover are exempt from the Privacy Act. In question b, the right option is the only hedged one, which gives it away.

proposal.title: Technology and global issues in setting up
card: A new business can use technology to build a customer database: a stored list of customer details, such as names, emails and past orders. It helps the business contact customers and see what they buy.

A database brings choices about data. The business should collect only the data it needs and keep it safe, as a data breach can harm customers and the business's reputation. Privacy law can also apply, depending on the business's size and type.
A business can also deal with overseas suppliers or sell to overseas retailers. This can lower the cost of goods or reach more customers, but it brings risks.

Exchange rates can change the price paid: if the Australian dollar falls in value, goods priced in another currency cost more. Shipping can also be slow or costly, and it is harder to check an overseas supplier's quality and standards.
proposal.remember: Technology and global dealings can help a new business, but each brings choices about data, cost and risk.

a.q: Priya opens an online shop in Geelong and stores her customers' names, emails and orders. Which choice does this database mainly bring?
opts: How to keep customer data safe and collect only what she needs
How to avoid the effect of exchange rate changes
How to set the steps for handling a staff complaint
How to pick a supplier with the lowest delivery price
a.why: A customer database holds personal details, so Priya should collect only what she needs and keep it safe, and privacy law can apply. Exchange rates matter when dealing overseas, not for a local database of customers.
a.clue: Think about what is stored in the database.

b.q: Sam's Melbourne café switches to an overseas supplier of coffee machines because the price is 20% lower. Which risk should Sam weigh before agreeing?
opts: The cost may rise if the Australian dollar falls in value
The cost may rise if the Australian dollar rises in value
Privacy law may apply to the coffee machines he buys
Overseas machines may be easier to check for quality
b.why: The supplier sets its price in another currency. If the Australian dollar falls, Sam needs more Australian dollars to pay the same price, which can cancel the saving. A rising Australian dollar does the opposite and makes the machines cheaper.
b.clue: Ask how much foreign money one Australian dollar can buy.
